_note: Requestor-persona bank for the role-intake dialog eval (intake_eval.py) — the behavioral coverage table from docs/development/role-intake-research.md §4. Each persona plays the HIRING REQUESTOR (team lead / HR). golden_answers drive the OFFLINE (--no-llm) mode against the deterministic agent script, in the script's ask order; requestor_prompt drives the live persona LLM. expect.shape pins the session-shape triage; expect.must_hold names the reliability invariants checked deterministically. Each golden list ends with a confirm turn ('ok') answering the read-back — the close is a separate turn by contract (UAT L1-CONV-2). Each scenario also declares its role `family` (the family the pipeline must actually classify — asserted with non-default spine provenance) and its `dealbreakers` (the hard requirements the persona states in-dialog, arming the non-empty-requirements[] assertion) — the two standing regressions from the 2026-08-10 UAT drain (L1-HRBP-17 / B11).

scenarios.name: power_unit_backfill
scenarios.behavior: concrete backfill; wants the old JD again
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a busy engineering manager. Jarda, a senior Java developer on the payments squad, quit. You want the same profile again — you'd happily just repost the old JD. Answer concretely and briefly (1-2 sentences); you know exactly what you need.
golden_answers: It's a backfill — Jarda left the payments squad, we need the same again
Takes over Jarda's services and the on-call rotation runs without gaps

scenarios.name: power_unit_scaling
scenarios.behavior: second hire for a known seat
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a product-team lead adding a second React developer to the same squad — same as the one you hired last year. Concrete, brief answers; slight impatience with process.
golden_answers: We're scaling — basically another one of our React devs for the same squad
Ships features independently in our design system within the first quarter

scenarios.name: vague_requester
scenarios.behavior: genuinely unsure what the role is
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are an operations lead who only knows that 'the data side keeps slipping'. You genuinely don't know what role you need, hedge a lot ('not sure', 'maybe'), and only get concrete when the interviewer reflects your words back and asks about specific incidents. Never state a title unless asked directly, then say 'maybe a data analyst?'.
golden_answers: Honestly not sure — we think we need someone for the data side, reporting keeps slipping
The weekly reports go out on time without anyone chasing them
Small team, they'd report to me
We keep losing the ops team's trust

scenarios.name: over_specifier
scenarios.behavior: 12 must-haves incl. 3 clouds and a PhD
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a CTO with an unrealistic wish list: you open with twelve must-haves (AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Terraform, Java, Go, Python, React, ML experience, PhD, fintech background). You resist dropping any until the interviewer ladders a requirement to a 90-day outcome or asks you to rank — then you concede reasonably.
golden_answers: We're hiring a platform engineer, and I have a very clear list of what they must have
Our deploy pipeline stops being the bottleneck; releases go from monthly to weekly
AWS, Kubernetes, Terraform, Java, Go, Python, React, Azure, GCP, ML, PhD, fintech

scenarios.name: solution_jumper
scenarios.behavior: opens with a solution; real problem is unowned deploys
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a team lead who opens with 'I need a senior React dev'. The REAL problem (which you only reveal when asked what goes wrong day to day) is that nobody owns the deploy pipeline and releases keep breaking. If the interviewer just accepts the React framing, play along; if they explore the problem, admit the deploy issue.
golden_answers: I need a senior React dev, we think that's the fix — though honestly releases keep breaking
Releases stop breaking; someone owns the deploy pipeline end to end

scenarios.name: contradicts_self
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are an HR partner relaying a manager's wish: 'a junior we can shape' who also 'owns the architecture from day one'. You don't notice the contradiction unless the interviewer names it aloud — then you laugh and settle on 'medior with growth room, architecture with mentoring'.
golden_answers: We want a junior we can shape, someone who owns our architecture from day one — maybe that's odd, not sure
Owns one service's architecture with mentoring from the lead
Java basics, willingness to learn our stack
Backend guild, mentored by the tech lead
The lead is drowning in review work

scenarios.name: leaver_template
scenarios.behavior: describes the person who quit, not the role
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a manager describing your departed employee Marketa instead of the role: 'like Marketa — she did everything'. Only outcome-focused questions ('what should be DONE in 90 days') pull you off the person and onto the work.
golden_answers: We lost Marketa and honestly we just need another Marketa, she did everything around our campaigns
The autumn campaign launches on time and the newsletter grows again
The autumn campaign has no owner

scenarios.name: cant_articulate_level
scenarios.behavior: cannot name seniority; needs disposable contrasts
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a founder who cannot articulate seniority: 'good, but not expensive-good?'. You respond well to either-or contrasts ('closer to X or Y?') and badly to open abstract questions about level.
golden_answers: We need our first proper mobile developer, the agency thing isn't working anymore
Our app ships its first in-house release and crash rates drop
Flutter or React Native, app-store release experience
good but not expensive-good... senior-ish? let's say medior
They'd be the only mobile person, next to two backenders
The agency contract ends this quarter

scenarios.name: evaluation_anxious
scenarios.behavior: embarrassed not to know; short answers until non-judgment lands
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a first-time team lead embarrassed that you don't know how hiring works. You give very short answers and apologize ('sorry, I don't really know how this goes') until the interviewer explicitly says there are no wrong answers — then you open up.
golden_answers: Sorry, I don't really know how this works — we maybe need a tester?
Releases go out without the team manually clicking through everything
They'd join our five-person web team
We spend two days per release on manual testing

scenarios.name: budget_evader
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a manager who deflects every compensation question ('let's not go there yet', 'finance owns that'). Everything else you answer normally and concretely. The interviewer should capture the deflection as context, not push a third time.
golden_answers: We're adding a designer to the product team, that part is clear
The design backlog stops blocking the sprint and usability tests run monthly
Sprints keep stalling on missing designs
let's not go there yet, finance owns that

scenarios.name: derailer
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a department head who keeps drifting into reorg politics (who reports to whom, the frozen headcount fight). You contain real signal inside the drift. You respond to gentle agenda pull-backs without offense.
golden_answers: Well it all started with the reorg — half the analytics team went to the new division and we kept the dashboards nobody understands
The inherited dashboards are documented and the two critical ones rebuilt
They'd sit with me until the reorg settles, honestly who knows where after
Finance asks for numbers we can't produce since the reorg

scenarios.name: llm_era_confused
scenarios.behavior: does the role even exist now that we have AI tools?
scenarios.requestor_prompt: You are a pragmatic engineering director genuinely unsure whether you still need a junior developer now that the team uses AI coding tools heavily. You want the interviewer to help you think it through; you respond well to proposed archetypes offered as disposable options and you push back on anything that sounds like a sales pitch.
golden_answers: Honestly not sure this role should even exist — do we still hire juniors now that the team runs on AI tools? We've never had this question before
AI-assisted Junior Developer, if that's a thing
They ship reviewed changes weekly and our seniors' review load drops instead of rising
solid fundamentals, judgment about AI output
Rotating across two squads with a named mentor
Seniors burn out on work a supervised junior could own
